stages.title: World War I and its global consequences
stages.hook: A single assassination in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 was followed within weeks by a war across several continents. Why did one event set so many states in motion?
explain: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary was the trigger, but long-term causes mattered: alliance systems, an arms build-up, imperial rivalries and nationalism in the Balkans. Within weeks, the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, later the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria) faced the Allies (France, Britain, Russia, later Italy, Japan, the United States and others).

The war was global. Over a million soldiers from India served overseas, and large numbers of troops and labourers came from Africa, the Caribbean, Indochina, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and China. Fighting took place in Europe, the Middle East, East Africa and the Pacific. Trench warfare on the Western Front caused huge losses, with roughly ten million military deaths. The armistice came on 11 November 1918.

The consequences were large. Four empires collapsed (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman). The Treaty of Versailles (1919) imposed terms on Germany, and the League of Nations began in 1920. Colonial peoples who had served expected change; many were disappointed, which fed later independence movements. The 1918 influenza pandemic then killed many millions more.

stages.title: Russian Revolution and Soviet history
stages.hook: In 1917 the world's largest country changed government twice in a single year. How did the Tsar's empire become the world's first communist state?
explain: Russia's heavy losses in World War I, food shortages and widespread unrest led to the February Revolution of 1917, in which Tsar Nicholas II abdicated. A Provisional Government continued the war. In October (November in the modern calendar) the Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power. A civil war followed (1918 to 1922), and the Soviet Union was formed in 1922.

Under Lenin the state nationalised industry, and later under Stalin it pursued rapid industrialisation and forced collectivisation of farms. A severe famine in 1932 to 1933, which killed millions, especially in Ukraine and Kazakhstan, followed. Many governments and historians recognise the Ukrainian famine, the Holodomor, as a genocide, while others see it as the result of brutal policy not aimed at Ukrainians as such; this is debated. The Great Terror of 1937 to 1938 saw mass arrests and executions, and the Gulag labour camps held millions.
The Soviet Union played a leading role in defeating Nazi Germany at great cost, then became one of two superpowers. It dissolved in December 1991, leaving 15 independent republics.

stages.title: World War II across Europe, Africa, Asia and the Pacific
stages.hook: World War II began in more than one place and at more than one time, depending on where you look. Why do historians date its start differently?
explain: In Asia, Japan invaded China in 1937 after fighting around the Marco Polo Bridge; in Europe, Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war. Germany defeated France in 1940, then invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941. The battles of Stalingrad (1942 to 1943) and El Alamein in North Africa (1942) turned the tide. Allied forces landed in Normandy on 6 June 1944, and Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945.

On 7 December 1941 Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and other targets, bringing the United States into the war and widening the Pacific war across Southeast Asia and the islands. Atomic bombs were used on Hiroshima (6 August 1945) and Nagasaki (9 August 1945), and Japan surrendered, with the formal ceremony on 2 September 1945.

The war was truly global. Troops from India, Africa, the Caribbean, Australia, China and many other places fought. Estimates suggest 70 to 85 million deaths, most of them civilians. It ended with the founding of the United Nations in 1945 and the start of the Cold War and of decolonisation.

stages.title: Holocaust and other documented mass atrocities
stages.hook: After 1945 the world created a new word and a new law for crimes aimed at destroying whole groups. What happened, and why is remembering it important?
explain: The Holocaust was the persecution and murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between 1933 and 1945, with most killings from 1941. Roma and Sinti people, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, and others were also murdered or persecuted. The Nazi state used laws, propaganda, ghettos, mass shootings and killing centres such as Auschwitz-Birkenau, which was liberated on 27 January 1945. The Nuremberg Trials (1945 to 1946) prosecuted leaders. In 1948 the UN adopted the Genocide Convention, based on the term created by Raphael Lemkin.

Other documented mass atrocities include the Armenian genocide of 1915 to 1923 in the Ottoman Empire, which killed about a million or more people and is recognised by many states and historians, though the Turkish state disputes the term; the German killing of Herero and Nama peoples in Namibia (1904 to 1908); the Khmer Rouge period in Cambodia (1975 to 1979); the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda in 1994; and the killing of more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica in 1995.

Historians study these events with documents, testimony and physical evidence. Survivors' accounts and memorials preserve the names and lives of victims, and education aims to help prevent such crimes.

example.q: Why is the evidence for the Holocaust so strong?
steps: The perpetrators left extensive records, orders and photographs.

example.a: Many independent kinds of evidence agree.

analogies.city: Memorial sites in cities keep names so victims are not reduced to numbers.
analogies.tech: Digital archives let students read survivors' testimonies.

stages.title: Decolonisation across Africa and Asia
stages.hook: In 1945 about a third of the world's people lived under colonial rule. By 1975 almost none did. How did this change happen so quickly?
explain: Decolonisation was driven by local movements and shaped by global change. After World War II, the imperial powers were weakened, and the UN's Charter spoke of self-determination. India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, with partition causing mass displacement and violence. Indonesia proclaimed independence in 1945 and gained recognition in 1949. Vietnam's forces defeated France at Dien Bien Phu in 1954.

In Africa, Ghana became independent in 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah, the first sub-Saharan colony to do so. In 1960, seventeen African states became independent. Paths varied: negotiated transitions in many British colonies, and long wars in Algeria (1954 to 1962), Kenya and later the Portuguese colonies, which won independence in 1974 and 1975 after a change of government in Portugal.

The Bandung Conference (1955) brought Asian and African leaders together. New states faced inherited borders, weak economies and sometimes Cold War pressures. Debates continue about whether economic dependence ('neocolonialism') persisted.

example.q: Why did independence come quickly in 1960 for many African states?
steps: Nationalist movements had grown strong.
European powers were weakened and costly wars deterred them.
Global opinion and the UN supported self-determination.
example.a: Strong movements met weakened, reluctant imperial powers.

stages.title: Cold War and international relations
stages.hook: For over forty years two superpowers never fought each other directly, yet wars took place in Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan. How did this 'cold' conflict work?
explain: After 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union emerged as superpowers with opposing systems: capitalism and liberal democracy versus communism and one-party rule. Europe was divided: the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan (1947) supported Western Europe, NATO formed in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955. The Berlin Blockade (1948 to 1949) and the Berlin Wall (built 1961) symbolised the split.

Nuclear weapons produced deterrence: neither side could attack without risking devastating retaliation. The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 brought the world close to nuclear war and was resolved by negotiation. Hotter conflicts took place by proxy, including the Korean War (1950 to 1953), the Vietnam War and wars in Africa and Afghanistan (1979 to 1989), causing great suffering in those regions.

Many newly independent states formed the Non-Aligned Movement. The Cold War ended as Eastern European regimes fell in 1989, the Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989, and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

example.a: Direct war was avoided; rivalry continued by other means.

stages.title: Civil rights and human rights movements
stages.hook: In 1948 the nations of the world agreed on a list of rights for every person. Yet millions still had to struggle to enjoy them. Why?
explain: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948. It set out rights for all people, though it was not legally binding. Movements around the world pressed for them to be real.

In the United States, the civil rights movement challenged racial segregation. Brown v. Board of Education (1954) held school segregation unconstitutional; the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955 to 1956) showed the power of mass nonviolent protest; the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) followed. Gandhi's method of nonviolent resistance had earlier influenced Indian independence and inspired others. In South Africa, resistance to apartheid grew through the African National Congress and others; Nelson Mandela was released in 1990 and elected president in 1994.

Other movements include women's suffrage (New Zealand gave women the national vote in 1893), the 1967 Australian referendum recognising Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the census and federal law-making, and Indigenous rights campaigns worldwide.

steps: Black residents, the majority of bus riders, stopped using the buses.

stages.title: Social, economic and cultural transformations
stages.hook: World population was about 2.5 billion in 1950 and passed 8 billion in 2022. What changes in food, health, work and technology made this possible?
explain: The 20th century saw rapid change. The Great Depression after 1929 led many governments to expand their role in the economy, and after World War II many built welfare states. Public health advances, such as vaccines and antibiotics, cut death rates, while the Green Revolution of the 1960s spread high-yield crops and fertilisers in Mexico, India and elsewhere, raising food output.

Cities grew rapidly worldwide, and migration increased within and between countries. Women entered paid work in growing numbers, and literacy rose. Radio, film, television and later the internet created shared popular cultures but also new inequalities and debates over cultural identity, as seen in movements to preserve Indigenous languages.
Economic globalisation expanded trade and finance, lifting many out of poverty, especially in East Asia, while inequality within and between countries remained and environmental pressures grew.

stages.title: Modern world history and historical source interpretation
stages.hook: Two newspapers from the same day report the same event very differently. How would a historian decide which to trust?
explain: Historians work with sources. Primary sources come from the time studied, such as letters, laws, photographs and oral testimony. Secondary sources, such as textbooks, interpret them. To judge a source, ask about its provenance (who made it, when and why), its purpose and audience, and its reliability. Corroboration, checking against independent sources, strengthens a claim.

Every source has a viewpoint. A government report, a soldier's diary, a colonial official's letter and an Indigenous oral account may each be valuable, yet each shows part of the story. Propaganda posters, for example, are poor evidence of what happened, but excellent evidence of what a government wanted people to believe.

Modern history includes the end of the Cold War (1989 to 1991), the attacks of 11 September 2001, the global financial crisis of 2008 and the COVID-19 pandemic from 2020. Digital media multiplies sources and misinformation, so source evaluation matters more than ever.

example.q: How would you assess a wartime poster as evidence?
steps: Identify who made it and why: a government to recruit or persuade.
Ask what it shows about aims and beliefs, not facts of events.
Compare with diaries, records and other independent sources.
example.a: It is strong evidence of intended messaging, weak evidence of events, until corroborated.

analogies.home: A family story told by one person may differ from another's; you ask both.
analogies.sport: Two fans of rival teams describe a match differently; a video replay is a check.
analogies.tech: A fact-checker compares claims with independent records.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: historians differ on how to weigh sources, and recent events have incomplete records because archives are not yet open.
